message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
I believe this is one of the strongest applications we have put together. The need is documented, not asserted: our household numbers are up by around two-thirds in two years, and we can quantify exactly how much fresh food we are turning away, 1.2 tonnes a week, because we log every declined offer. The project responds directly to that gap and nothing more. The budget is lean: we got competing quotes for the cold room and the electrics and took the lower figure each time, and the van comes with a warranty. The value for money is exceptional, at roughly 33p per meal in the first year and falling to almost nothing over the equipment's ten-year life. We have thought about the long term too: this is a one-off capital investment with written supermarket commitments behind it, so it will keep delivering without coming back to funders. Our monitoring is concrete and measurable. I am confident the Foundation will see this as exactly the kind of lasting capacity-building its fund exists for.
</author>

The review is to check that the recommendation is clear and the document is ready to go to the decision-makers.

<document>
Grant Application: Chilled Storage for Fresh Food Distribution
Applicant: Hollins Valley Food Bank (registered charity)
To: Ashworth Community Foundation, Community Resilience Fund (capital grants)
Amount requested: £48,600

1. About us
Hollins Valley Food Bank has provided emergency food to households in the valley since 2014. We are run by two part-time paid staff and around 70 volunteers, and we operate from a warehouse in Hollinsford and three distribution sites in Hollinsford, Brackley Bridge and Over Hollins, which open on different days of the week. Referrals come from GPs, schools, Citizens Advice and the local authority's welfare team.

2. The need
Demand has risen sharply. The number of households we supported rose from an average of 410 a week in 2023 to 620 a week in 2025, an increase of 66%. Over the same period our food donations have changed in character. Supermarket surplus schemes now offer us large volumes of fresh produce, dairy and chilled ready meals, but we have no chilled storage beyond three domestic fridges, so we currently decline around 1.2 tonnes of fresh food each week. Our parcels are therefore dominated by tinned and dried goods, and clients, referrers and our own volunteers consistently tell us that families want fresh food, particularly for children.

3. The project
We are seeking funding to:
- install a 12 cubic metre walk-in cold room at our Hollinsford warehouse;
- buy a used refrigerated van, so that chilled food can be collected from supermarket depots and taken to our four distribution sites at safe temperatures;
- upgrade the warehouse electrical supply to support the cold room.

With these in place we could accept the 1.2 tonnes a week we currently decline, about 62 tonnes a year. Using the national food-redistribution conversion of 2,380 meals per tonne, that is around 147,600 additional meals a year, at a one-off capital cost of about 33p per meal in the first year alone.

4. Budget
Item | Cost
Walk-in cold room, supply and installation | £26,400
Refrigerated van (three years old, 40,000 miles) | £18,500
Electrical supply upgrade | £3,700
Total requested | £48,600

Quotes from two suppliers were obtained for the cold room and the electrical work; the lower quote is shown in each case. The van price is from a commercial dealer and includes a 12-month warranty.

5. Running costs
We have obtained estimates for the additional running costs. The cold room will add around £4,200 a year to our electricity bill. Insurance, fuel, servicing and road tax for the van will cost around £6,800 a year. Our 2025 accounts show total income of £96,000, almost all of it restricted to food purchasing and staff costs, an unrestricted surplus of £900, and unrestricted reserves of £5,100.

6. Outcomes and monitoring
We will measure:
- tonnes of fresh and chilled food received and distributed each month;
- the proportion of parcels containing fresh produce (currently under 10%; target 80% within six months);
- client feedback through our quarterly survey.
We will report to the Foundation at six and twelve months.

7. Timetable
The cold room supplier can install within eight weeks of order. We would order on award, with the cold room and van in service by October 2026.

8. Sustainability
This is a one-off capital investment. Once installed, the cold room and van will be sustainable without further grant funding, and will serve the valley for at least ten years. Our partner supermarkets have confirmed in writing that they will continue to offer us surplus fresh food.

9. Why fund us
The Foundation's Community Resilience Fund aims to strengthen local organisations' long-term capacity to meet need. This project does exactly that: a modest capital investment that permanently transforms the quality of the food we can give to families, at a very low cost per meal.
</document>
response:
# Review: Hollins Valley Food Bank chilled storage application

**Verdict: not ready to send yet.** The ask is clear (£48,600 for a cold room, van and electrics), and the need case is strong. But the sustainability section is contradicted by the application's own figures, and an assessor will spot that quickly. There are also a percentage error, an internal inconsistency and an out-of-date timetable. Each is fixable in an afternoon.

## Must fix before submission

**1. Running costs can't be met from your current finances.**
Section 5 gives new running costs of about **£11,000 a year** (£4,200 electricity plus £6,800 van). The same section shows:
- an unrestricted surplus of **£900**
- unrestricted reserves of **£5,100**
- income almost all restricted to food and staff

On these figures, the running costs would use up all your reserves within about six months. Section 8 still says the project "will be sustainable without further grant funding." An assessor reading sections 5 and 8 together will doubt the project, and possibly the organisation's financial planning.

The application needs a credible funding plan for the £11,000 a year. For example:
- a supermarket or depot contribution toward collection costs
- a confirmed or applied-for revenue grant
- a costed fundraising target
- some saving on purchased food, since more donated fresh food may reduce what you buy

If you can't name a source yet, say so honestly and describe the plan. Remove "sustainable without further grant funding." Also check whether the Foundation's capital fund requires evidence that running costs are covered, as many do.

**2. The growth figure is wrong.**
410 to 620 households a week is an increase of **51%**, not 66%. (210 ÷ 410 = 0.51.) Your summary repeats the error as "around two-thirds." Change it to "just over 50%" or "half as many again." The real figure is still a strong case, and a visible arithmetic error in the first evidence paragraph undermines the "documented, not asserted" strength you rely on.

**3. Three or four distribution sites?**
Section 1 lists **three** sites (Hollinsford, Brackley Bridge, Over Hollins). Section 3 says the van will serve "our **four** distribution sites." Reconcile these. If the warehouse counts as a fourth site, say so.

**4. The timetable has passed.**
Section 7 says the equipment will be "in service by October 2026," which is already behind us. Restate it relative to the award, e.g. "cold room and van in service within 10–12 weeks of award." Or give a realistic date based on the Foundation's decision cycle.

## Should fix

**5. The cost-per-meal claim is overstated.**
- **33p excludes running costs.** Including year-one running costs, the figure is (£48,600 + £11,000) ÷ 147,600 ≈ **40p**. That is still excellent value. Quote it honestly, or label 33p as "capital cost only."
- **"Falling to almost nothing" isn't true.** Ongoing running costs are about **7.5p per meal** every year (£11,000 ÷ 147,600). That is still very good, but it is not nothing. This phrase is in your summary, not the document, so keep it out of any cover note.

**6. The ten-year life claim doesn't fit the van.**
A three-year-old van with a 12-month warranty will not plausibly serve for "at least ten years." Say the cold room has a 10+ year life and the van an expected 5–7 years. Better still, mention how you would replace it. Assessors also tend to ask why there is only one van quote when the other items had two. Either get a second quote or explain why not.

**7. The supermarket commitment is weaker than it sounds.**
"Will continue to offer us surplus fresh food" is not a volume commitment. If the letters mention quantities or frequency, quote them and attach the letters. If they don't, soften the wording so it isn't presented as a guarantee.

**8. The 80% target is very ambitious.**
Going from under 10% to 80% of parcels with fresh produce in six months is a big jump. Check it works: 1.2 t across 620 households is about 1.9 kg per household per week, which looks feasible. But supply will vary. Consider a phased target, e.g. 50% at six months and 75% at twelve. Missing a stretch target looks worse than beating a realistic one.

## Worth a sentence each

- **Who drives the van and runs the collections?** You have two part-time staff. Name the driver and the volunteer rota for collecting and handling an extra 1.2 tonnes a week.
- **Food safety at distribution sites.** The sites open on different days. Explain how chilled food stays at safe temperatures once it arrives at a site, e.g. delivered on the day of distribution or kept in cool boxes.
- **Monitoring.** Add a baseline and target for the client survey, and offer an annual tonnage report beyond month twelve. This supports your long-term-capacity argument.

## What's already strong

- The need evidence: the logged declined offers giving 1.2 t a week is excellent and specific.
- The capital budget is clear, with competing quotes on two of the three items.
- The meals conversion and capital-cost arithmetic are correct (62 t × 2,380 ≈ 147,600 meals; £48,600 ÷ 147,600 ≈ 33p).
- The fit with the fund's purpose is well argued in section 9.

**Priority order:** 1 (running costs), then 2–4 (quick factual fixes), then 5–6 (claims an assessor will test). Fixing item 1 properly will matter more to the decision than everything else combined.
